utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We will now hear the submissions of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon all the parties in the proceedings. In July 2003, when Mr. Sljivacanin was to state his plea in regard to the indictment for the first time and in the absence of counsel he pleaded not guilty. Today, when it is upon us to close this chapter and hand over all the pages of the records and documents to solely your hands, Your Honours, at the end of my closing argument I shall reiterate these words of his with my deepest conviction that that will be your decision as well. I should like to remind you that in his opening words at the beginning of this trial, Sljivacanin said that he wanted his truth all about Ovcara to also become your truth, because the truth about Ovcara is needed by all who are not afraid of it. It is needed by the families of the victims, by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, the families of the killed soldiers and officers and the Serbian and Croatian public, the Guards Brigade, and it is also needed by Veselin Sljivancanin and his family. You have received in the closing arguments two versions of the event, a version of the Prosecution which we foresaw in certain form, and even though the Prosecution in his closing arguments surprised us with some of his new theses, quite contrary to his earlier positions, nonetheless we cannot expect the Prosecutor to do anything else but do his job within the framework of the mandate, and trusted him, and that mandate is to prosecute. As regards that method of the Prosecution's contribution to the exercise of his mandate, Prosecution and the primacy of prosecution of the truth, we shall be discussing that today, but we expected that. That is an attack looking the other party in the eye. That is an attack applying the Machiavellian approach, namely that the end justifies the means, whatever the means. But then you also have received and have before you another version of the events, the version of the Defence of Mr. Mrksic, his Defence team. This is a version that we did not expect, and I believe that the Prosecutor himself did not expect it. This is a version which the Defence team kept in its custody within the confines of its notes and folders avoiding to present evidence in that respect or to confront it with the witnesses in the courtroom and on behalf of history as they claim to actually place it in its proper place after the close of the evidentiary procedure. It is quite normal that that blow, the blow that you sustain with the other parties not looking you in the eye, is all the harder and all the more painful, but we are not afraid of the pain, we who want to establish the truth and not afraid of such pain. These approaches did not intimidate a single -- also did not intimidate one of the witnesses for the Defence, Mr. Sljivacanin, and not a single witness for the Defence of Mr. Sljivacanin who came here to publicly take the witness stand among the -- those who -- from whom the teams of the Prosecutor and Mrksic fled away although they had courageously placed them on their lists of potential witnesses. We shall be drawing attention to that also in our closing argument and to the specific and selective approach in the evidentiary procedure in regard of the presented version of events. Now we have occasion to inform you of our own version of events. We sought in our closing arguments not to impose any conclusions, not by way of logic, which is the favourite approach of Mr. Moore in his closing arguments nor by way of inferences or conclusions on allegations outside the evidentiary procedures -- procedure, as directed to do by Mr. Vasic. In our closing argument, and today here we have decided to speak primarily with a desire to remind and point -- remind of and point to everything that has been heard here during the trial in the respective cases and not outside it. We analysed from the angle of the defence for Mr. Sljivacanin the evidence and the evidentiary claims, both those which are in favour and those which are not in favour of Mr. Sljivacanin. Your conclusion on this trial may and must be based solely on the factual allegations which were heard during this trial in this courtroom. The question which is before you is whether such claims shall suffice for you to draw a conclusion on the existence of the criminal liability of the accused, and even more so whether they shall suffice for the establishment of the full truth about the crime at Ovcara. The professional burden and the task that you face is primarily to analyse the testimonies of witnesses as the most voluminous portion of the presented evidence, and there, in assessing their testimonies, you will be confronted with a major problem, that is the reliability and the cogency, the compelling nature of the descriptions of events that took place 15 years ago, 15 years before they were -- the evidence on them was presented. And apart from that, in respect of almost all the witnesses you also have their earlier statements before you and transcripts from other trials about this particular event. I believe that during the proceedings not a single witness appeared without the parties pointing to certain contradictions of such witnesses in respect of their previous accounts. There were witnesses both on the Prosecution's on the Defence's side who had given six or even previous statements before. All the parties in the proceedings, where it suited their thesis and what the witness had stated in his prior statement, always asked the cliche question, "Do you agree with me that your memory earlier had been fresher with respect to that particular event than it is today?" So this is vitally tenable and logical thesis, but the prior statements of the witnesses actually have a trap hidden in them, and this is something which has not been overlooked nor neglected by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Such statements have been taken by the method of entering into the record responses without the questions of those who is doing the interviewing, especially when those questions were leading and directed to support the interests, to corroborate the thesis of the interviewer. This was actually the Prosecution's favourite approach to the taking of statements. Although we know from their practice that the Prosecutors record all conversations or interviews and that they have audio regarding of them, we were submitted only several such recordings during this trial. When we asked them to submit to us the audio recording of Witness P-009, they just informed us that one didn't exist. The signature of the witness, Your Honours, is not at all in doubt, nor whether it is the witness's offered the possibility to enter any corrections prior to signing statements. What is in doubt, what is disputable, and that is a key in respect of key topics, is what the interviewer asks and how the question is formulated and how the answer is formulated. Corroborating this submission of ours is the enormous number of the addenda of Prosecution witnesses with respect to their prior statements. We are underlining all this, and we have pointed this in our opening arguments also, that due to the lapse of time and the precise questions which we were interested in with reason that documents have become an important source for two of your tasks. First, you can establish facts on that basis with reliability, and on the other hand you can verify the credibility of witnesses. Documents, as has been shown, have become during this trial the means of our struggle for the truth, and for some other people they have become a problem in grappling with the same truth. Now I'm going to move to some other questions which were also raised these days in the closing arguments, and I shall just limit myself to the key issues, wishing not to repeat what has already been written. First I shall say a few words about the place of the security organs in the structure of the JNA and specifically the Vukovar operation, namely whether by virtue of his function Sljivacanin has command function primarily in respect of the military police. In their final -- in their closing arguments, the Prosecution seems to forget what they claimed in the indictment and what their own military experts claimed. At that time, the Prosecutor claimed that Sljivacanin did not have any de jure ordering position vis-a-vis anybody, and this is something that the Prosecutor decidedly asserts, including not towards the military police, and this ambiguously emanates from the relevant regulations. I have given a detailed explanation of this in our final brief, and I'm not going to dwell on the subject now. What should be pointed out is the significance difference, distinction, from the jobs in which the organ of security is the actual holder of the office, the actual vehicle of the function, and those in which he just participates. Obviously this is a difference that neither the Prosecutor nor the Defence team of Mr. Mrksic wanted to notice, because both the Prosecutor and Mr. Mrksic's Defence team know full well that the -- this transport and security of POWs exclusively the task of the military police and that in such jobs, the unit of the military police as well in other jobs, it is exclusively subordinated to its commander. The Prosecutor actually suppresses this fact through the construction about the de jure position of Sljivacanin in the evacuation of the hospital, while Mr. Mrksic's Defence team compounds that with another construction yet, namely that the organs of security are only competent for POWs, and the only ones competent for POWs, and that that was done outside the command and the command chain, and that the commander knew nothing about it. To their regret it is just not so, because the evidence and the regulations and the documents and the testimonies actually show that it is quite the opposite. The job of evacuation including POWs is solely within the remit of the command line of the unit, and it is implemented through subordinated units, primarily the military police. In the service of the organs of security there is no reference whatsoever about POWs, and whereas regulations for the military police do make such references in contrast, and it is quite clear to whom the military police is subordinated. There is another thing which is sought to be mystified, which is the procedure to detect persons who are potential perpetrators of criminal offences against armed forces and the constitutional order. They -- this is sought to be represented as the exclusive job of the OB from the lowest to the highest level, and thereby as far as possible from the command structure of the unit. What is important in that thesis is to portray the absence of the existence -- to portray the existence of some parallel chain of command in the structure of the organs of security. No, there is no parallel command chain, and that is quite clear also from the report of the expert Theunens and his expertise on page 81. A significant number of documents have been tendered on the activities of the organs of security which relate to information on the -- about the adversarial side. Yes, there existed reports which were received from different sources on individuals who were the subject of interest of organs of security specifically with relation to their own ambit. Yes, these are reports, Your Honours, which the OB received, and they were important information for the commanding officers' structure also because they were indeed sent in order for the commanding officers to acquaint themselves with them in order to plan combat operations. That is evidence A 2485. Those documents show that -- that there were unambiguous indications that the hospital was not being used only for its primary function, that members of the ZNG and the MUP were hiding there, that it was being used as hideout by these persons and that after the end of combat they disguised themselves as civilians and wounded. This was explicitly confirmed for our benefit by Mr. Moore two days ago as well. I will not be invoking those specific documents. They have been pointed out in our brief. What is a security organ expected to do, having received that type of information and instruction, lists, data, sketches? Sljivacanin and the security organs did what they had to do. They performed their task under the regulations and pursuant to orders from their commander. They had a duty to track down any such persons, and they had a duty to contribute to setting up the conditions for a safe evacuation of the wounded and sick. That was all they did, and they did no more than that. However, never for a moment, and this is something that I wish to underline, did they shy away from their task. And this is what Sljivacanin told me when I met him. I mentioned that in my opening argument. He said, "If I am to answer for what I did, and if that is a crime, then the Court must establish that and tell me as much." The Defence submits what Mr. Sljivacanin did in his capacity as a security organ and a JNA officer is no crime. Everything was done in compliance with the regulations including those relate together security organs, and for as long as everything was done in compliance with those rules no crime occurred nor did Mr. Sljivacanin or the security organ have anything at all to do with the crime. It was only pursuant to an approval of his own commander or his order could a security organ go about their work in the proper way. Their work was not independent of the chain of command. It is primarily used for the needs and purposes of the chain of command, and it has to do with the safety and security of the units. The security organ reports primarily to their own commander under Article 12, Exhibit 107. This article makes no distinction whatsoever in relation to cases where a commander is simply denied information. As for the duty of transporting and securing prisoners, that is not counter-intelligence work and nothing for the security organ, as Mr. Vasic says in paragraph 138 of his own brief. It is true that the remit of the security organ is to track down persons undermining the armed forces and the constitutional order. However, first and foremost, it is the chain of command that has a duty of security transport and ensuring that such persons are safe. Let us have a look at who ordered the 80th Motorised Brigade to secure the Mitnica group. The commander of the brigade. Who from the 80th Brigade made the decision regarding the -- the hangar appointing Danilovic as camp commander? Who did Vezmarovic report to when he arrived from Sremska Mitrovica about having completed that task and the lists that he typed up on the morning of the 19th, as he claims? Who ordered the security organs to be present at Velepromet as early as the 27th of October? At least that's what Exhibit 401 suggests. Who received word of the fact that the ZNG and MUP were disguising themselves in the hospital? And this is the commander's daily report, Exhibit 401. Who informed accordingly the command of the 1st Military District and SSNO, Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence cabinet? Why did Colonel Mrksic in his daily report dated the 18th of November, Exhibit 417, write that activities were being carried out in order to select and distinguish the civilian population from the Ustashas? And then, if we look at Exhibit 418, which is another regular report, daily report, there is word of a selection being in progress in the Vucedol area and a group of the Croat forces, Ustashas, being put together in the Velepromet area; that was the expression used. Finally, if prisoners of war and processing prisoners of war were not within the remit of the of the command, or the commander, on the critical date the 28th [as interpreted] of November, why then did Colonel Mrksic write the following in Exhibit 421, his regular daily report at 1800 hours? He wrote that a selection was carried out and that many Ustasha were discovered hidden among the civilians, mingling with the civilians, and that the selection process was conducted in full compliance with the Geneva Conventions. We all know what the only selection process was on the 28th [as interpreted] of November, the one taking place at the hospital. It should be the 20th of November, page 10, line 24. If tracking down prisoners of war, selecting them and transporting them is within the exclusive remit of the security organ in this notorious chain of command, why then are there such precise references about this in the report by the commander who was part of the regular chain of command? The answer is quite simple. There is no need to look for answers in the -- in the realm of imaginary security associations. The security detail and its organs did their own job within the function of their command at all levels. There is something else I wish to say. One of the things that Mr. Moore discovers and one of the theories espoused for the first time in his final brief is that Sljivacanin was in charge and in command of all previous evacuations, including those that took place in October, the one organised by the Medecins Sans Frontiere, as well as the one on the 18th of November at Mitnica and the 19th of November at Velepromet. Mr. Moore, that is quite clear, had to weigh this up carefully and think carefully about whether he wished to make this theory public now, at the very end of our trial. One thing that was a potential trouble for him was no doubt the fact that in all these evacuations the actions taken by the JNA and officers of the JNA were positive steps to help conduct the evacuation. These are facts that so contradict his own theory on the existing plan and the joint criminal enterprise. However, in making this assessment, Mr. Moore find out that he did not have sufficient evidence on Sljivacanin's own command function in the context of the 20th of November evacuation. Therefore, he had to create some sort of foundation. Why would Sljivacanin of all people be put in charge of this evacuation? Which is exactly what Mr. Moore does. "Sljivacanin," he says, "was in order of all the previous evacuations. It was only logical for him to be in charge of the one that occurred on the 20th as well." Unfortunately that was not the case. Sljivacanin was involved in the October evacuation to the extent that anyone was. This was part of his work as a security organ. Even Mr. Theunens confirmed in his report that security organs were actively involved in the evacuations. This is paragraph 76 and the page is 10718. Sljivacanin gave ample evidence in his own testimony about his own involvement in these evacuations. However, Mr. Moore never asked him a single question about the October evacuation, which in itself shows that his theory on the purported command role of the Sljivacanin as early as October only ever occurred to him as he was drafting his final brief. I will not be speaking any long better October evacuation, but there has been ample evidence about that during the trial. I would like to draw your attention to Exhibit 829, which is a video clip. There was security assessments to the effect that the Croatian side would misuse the October convoy for their own ends. All the more reason for the security organ to be actively involved in escorting that evacuation. These are exhibits 408 and 878. Mr. Moore knows this full well, or perhaps he chooses to forget, but what is particularly indicative is that in paragraph 530, when claiming that Sljivacanin was in command of the October evacuation, in his footnote 1653, Mr. Moore invokes the evidence of Dr. Bosanac, Kolesar, and Njavro. This was not something that I was able to actually find in their statements. As for the November 18 evacuation the Defence have provided our own arguments in our brief. We have a new position, by Mr. Moore again, which is quite contrary to what he says in his pre-trial brief and the opening argument, namely that here again Sljivacanin was in command. As to fact, based on which one could ascertain who was in charge of that evacuation, this is clearly established based on such evidence as has been produced, and cannot be established based on circumstantial evidence and constructions. The security and transport of the prisoners was something that was done by the members of the 2nd Battalion of the military police, Paunovic, and the 3rd JOD under the command of Major Stupar, Exhibit 831 specifically. As for organising, securing, and accepting up -- or, rather, appointing the camp commander at Ovcara, as well as the dismantling of the Ovcara camp, we all know this Exhibit 371. These are all fundamental decisions made in relation to the evacuation because of Commander Vojnovic. These were orders from the commander to his own units. That is the only fact there is. That is a model, and that is the form that the evacuation actually took. How it was organised and the hospital evacuation was supposed to follow the same pattern, the same model. I would like to ask the Court to please go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can be reliably concluded on the basis of important documents and competent witnesses is once again something that the Prosecutor does not wish to accept, let alone tell you that. Here when it comes to evacuation the key role in negotiations, surrender, and evacuation, was played by Colonel Pavkovic. He led that process, he did a good job, and his efforts were recognised, and this is something that is publicly known. He led negotiations. He informed the command about negotiations. According to his information, commander issued an order. Please look at Exhibit 401, dated 18th of November at 1400 hours and 1430, where they speak of Mitnica. Mr. Moore saw this but he decided to ignore it. Pavkovic came and supervised the departure of the Mitnica group on the 19th of November. This is something that the Prosecution witness, Vojnovic, testified about, transcript page 9080. The conclusion of the Prosecution that the Guards Brigade once again did everything in accordance with the regulations with the presence of the International Red Cross is fully tendentious. The International Red Cross namely Mr. Borsinger were present at negotiations and surrender of the Mitnica group only on the 18th. They were not present at Ovcara. They were not present when the organisation of the evacuation of civilians was done. However, everything was done in accordance with regulations and international standards. It was done in a professional, humane, and dedicated way involving soldiers and officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade, regardless of whether they were supervised by the International Red Cross or not. Similar to the evacuation on the 18th of November, from the documents and from the testimony one can easily glean the role of Sljivacanin in the evacuation on the 19th, and it is clear that he had no command role in that evacuation. The Prosecutor forgets that the Velepromet facility was organised as a reception centre much earlier than the 19th of November and that several evacuations were organised from that location by way of which civilians left the war area. This is something that Dr. Vesna Bosanac was fully aware of when she insisted that civilians did not come to the hospital and that they should go to Velepromet. Prosecution witness P-301, page 3533, spoke about this, as well as Tanja Dosen and Dr. Bosanac herself, page 7121.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness P-031, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even though it doesn't quite suit Witness Bosanac now, she firmly confirmed before the Court that she did not complain to Borsinger about the fact that civilians were taken away on the 19th, of which she was fully aware at the time. Page 860 and 861. It must be that Dr. Bosanac was aware of other things as well, namely that at the time on the 19th in the afternoon at the hospital there were already many members of ZNG and MUP. They were disguising themselves, that somehow they had to be included in the evacuation of the wounded and the sick, and that the presence of the large number of civilians at the hospital at that time was actually a hindrance in that process. As for the conflict between Sljivacanin and Borsinger, which allegedly existed before the incident on the bridge only the 20th of November, actually was never there. Now I'm going to remind you of the body language that Mr. Moore insisted upon in order to show the arrogance of Sljivacanin in Exhibit 318 and his constant belligerent attitude. Your Honours, do you know why Mr. Moore did not play the audio feed when he played that tape to support this argument? Because audio feed spoils his argument about the alleged constant obstruction of Sljivacanin and -- in relation to the International Red Cross. In the dialogue, that we have seen so many times during this trial from opening arguments on, I think that all of us by now know it by heart. So in that footage Borsinger says, "I'm used to better cooperation," when Sljivacanin addressed him. So it is Borsinger who claims before cameras that he had good cooperation with the JNA. That's how it was on the 18th and on the 19th. Please remember who put journalists in touch with Borsinger. That's something that van Lynden testified about. Sljivacanin testified about that as well. This shows the friendly relationship between Sljivacanin, Borsinger, which the Prosecutor cynically put under quotation marks. This is something that Borsinger confirmed himself. Velepromet was never within the jurisdiction of Sljivacanin or the JNA. The Prosecutor misinterpreted Exhibit 835 in order to support this argument. Please pay careful attention to the content of that exhibit, and the jobs performed by Borisavljevic in order to uncover extremists and members of ZNG and MUP is something that is used to attribute effective control to Sljivacanin over those facilities. There is no evidence to support this. The document that the Prosecutor invokes and the documents that we supplied to you show something quite the opposite. In that facility there were absolutely no problems before the night of the 19th of November. This is something that even the Prosecutor acknowledges in the indictment, because they charged Mrksic and Sljivacanin with the knowledge about the crime which took place in the night of -- on the 19th of November, paragraph 31. Once again here, the Defence points out a very important detail when it comes to mens rea of Sljivacanin and security at Velepromet. Had there indeed been something in relation to the crime at Velepromet that Sljivacanin knew about or supposed about, would he have taken that -- there on that same day in the morning Cyrus Vance and a delegation including so many journalists? On that occasion Mr. Vance had unhindered talks with civilians who were present there. Exhibit 69, 70, and 861. Had the evacuation task from Velepromet indeed been within the competence of Sljivacanin, as the Prosecutor claims, and had it been the case, as Mr. Vasic claimed, that this was within the competence of the security organ, then this would not have been within the competence of the Operations Group South command, Exhibit 418. The work of all security organs at the Velepromet, at the hospital, and on the following day, and at Vucedol on the previous day, was exactly the way it was described in Exhibit 401 in the entry that is there, and you will remember that this was something described by the people from the security administration who came there. It says there that they came there to perform the selection and separation of the members of armed forces of Croatia from civilian population, full stop. Transport, security, and surrender is something that was done by other organs of the command of the 1st Military District. When it comes to Velepromet, we have to highlight in several words something that was described in detail in our final brief. Rather, I'm now going to tell you that famous sentence of the witness, Vujic, which was mentioned here for the first time before you, even though from 1999 he testified more than four times. Allegedly Sljivacanin told him, "Don't be surprised if some Chetnik there cuts a throat of some Ustasha there." I'm going to tell you now something that Mr. Moore said, namely that Mr. Korica is an honourable and decent officer, and is a friend of Mr. Vujic. Mr. Korica firmly denies that he heard that sentence uttered, even though he was present when they met. But Vujic himself is the one who impeaches his own testimony. Page 4785, especially page 4795, show that his own testimony at the trial in Belgrade was put to him in the trial against the accused Vujanovic, et al. There, Vujic stated that he was surprised by the presence of Chetniks at the Velepromet because nobody told them previously that they could come across some Chetniks there, and also that nobody told him that they could encounter anything unpleasant there. The view of the Defence is that this was stated very clearly and reliably. This is recorded on an audiotape, and this is an unequivocal statement. However, Vujic was unable to explain before this Trial Chamber the discrepancy when this comes to this sentence that was now uttered for the first time, and that was not that he had just remembered it. No. He claimed quite the opposite. Sljivacanin did not utter that sentence. This was firmly confirmed by Korica. In that portion of his testimony, Vujic is unconvincing and confused. The addendum with this sentence was provided at the time when the Prosecution kept trying to include the events in Velepromet in the incriminating deeds in the indictment. Now let us turn to the question which is truly fundamental for the Defence of Mr. Sljivacanin and his criminal liability. Was he appointed commander of the evacuation of the hospital both including wounded and ill and the persons that were separated between hospital and Ovcara, and did he, by that fact, have de jure command authority over all the persons included in this? All joint passionate arguments both of the Prosecution and Mr. Mrksic's Defence with the same conclusion is something that we heard and read. The Prosecution needs to prove that Sljivacanin was de jure competent for the evacuation of the hospital because the authority was delegated to him by the commander, and the Prosecution needs to do that because they're deeply aware of the fact that looking at his function and position, Sljivacanin did not have such command responsibility. The Defence of Mr. Mrksic needs to remove Mr. Mrksic as far away from the evacuation as possible including the evacuation of the wounded and sick, and they need to show he had no responsibilities whatsoever over transport, security, and the accommodations of prisoners of war. Can the commander transfer his competencies to one of the subordinate commanders. Certain regulations allowed for such a delegation of authority both in writing and verbally; however, the rules of service of security organs did not allow that tasks be issued to the security organ by the commander that fall outside of his scope of work. This is Article 48, Exhibit 107. Is this selection and separation of persons something that is within the scope of work of the security organ. The position of the Defence is that it is. Is the transport and security of prisoners of war and evacuation of the wounded and sick something that falls within the scope of work of security organ? The position of the Defence is that it is not. According to the regulations, was Mrksic authorised to appoint Major Sljivacanin for commander of the evacuation of the hospital? Our position is that he wasn't. Was a special written decision necessary for such unlawful decision? Well, Prosecution Witness Trifunovic, who was considered as expert here, and I fully agree with that, firmly says on page 8324 that such a written decision was necessary. What is now even more striking in the final brief of the Prosecutor in supporting such a thesis is Mr. Moore's approach to the necessity of essential decisions being in the required written form and the invocation of experts Vuga and Pringle in his brief in paragraph 81 and foot into the 363 to that effect. In accomplishing this aim, the Prosecutor actually applies different standards in interpreting the regulations. For resubordination, according to him, a written decision is necessary, and for tasks which are beyond the remit and the -- for the tasks which are within the operation of the evacuation of the hospital, they do not matter. You have read Vasic's thesis in his own brief talking about being already at tasks of selection and triage with which, according to him, the commander has nothing to do whatsoever. Sljivacanin was appointed also commander of the evacuation by an oral order of the 19th of November, which, as Vasic claims in paragraph 185 of his final brief, all the commanding officers heard at the daily meeting. What commanding officers? Paunovic was not [as interpreted] at all at the meeting. Susic was at the meeting; he didn't hear it. Gluscevic, a member of the command, had to be at that meeting. A correction. I apologise to the interpreters. It is page 21, line 25. Paunovic was at the meeting, and Gluscevic, a member of the command, had to be at the meeting, a witness of Mr. Mrksic's Defence. Mr. Vasic just didn't ask him about that. Lesanovic, a command member, was at the meeting, also was not asked about it by anyone. He was not asked by Mr. Vasic, who is actually advancing this thesis. Vojnovic doesn't know anything about the evacuation. We heard that from his testimony here and he was a member of the command and went to the meetings. No questions are being asked about the thesis that needs to be proven. The facts in this case are established on the basis of testimonies and presented evidences rather than on the basis of assertions in the briefs, in the submissions. And, finally, both the Prosecution and Mr. Mrksic's Defence in asserting this thesis solely and exclusively invoke the testimony of Witness Panic from his statement, which he gave to the OTP in 2005. That is indicative, namely that both the Defence of Mr. Mrksic and the OTP have placed Mr. Panic on the list of their potential witnesses but they abandoned it very hastily. I mean the idea. The Defence of Sljivacanin claims, and this was also demonstrated during his testimony, that both Mr. Moore and Mr. Vasic knew full well what Panic would testify, what documents that they had shown him, and what documents they had not shown him within the proofing process, and how important it was for him -- for -- for them for him not to appear before the Court. You saw during this two days how painful for them was the testimony of Mr. Panic, and you saw that from both their final submissions and their closing arguments. And what was it that Mr. Panic actually testified in relation to the task of the evacuation of the hospital? He clearly testified before this Court that Sljivacanin had been issued a precise task by the commander, and that was to separate persons suspected of having participated in combat operations and to put in place safe conditions for the evacuation of the wounded and sick. That is transcript 14294-5. Sljivacanin was issued -- received no command function at all over the evacuation of the hospital, and nobody heard anything of the kind at the command held in OG South on the 19th of November, 1991. What he was issued was a task from his own remit like other organs received -- were assigned tasks from their own fields of competence. The logistics to ensure transportation, military police to secure the operation, the Medical Corps to examine the sick and the wounded. So Panic and all the other participants in the evacuation adamantly testified that on that day Sljivacanin did not issue any orders to them at all, and that, as regards their tasks which they had been assigned and which they were implementing, they never reported on them to Sljivacanin but to the person who had issued them the task, their commander, Mrksic. The facts attest to that, the testimonies attest to that, and not the statements -- these statements which were taken in a quite problematic way. And as regards how the statement -- how Panic's statement was taken, the statement which is now treated as the only source of the OTP assertion and the Defence of Mr. Mrksic's assertion on the alleged de jure command function of Sljivacanin, and that is transcript 14546 to 48, will be weighed properly, as we said at the beginning of our closing arguments, by this Tribunal by judging the assertions in the prior statement, a statement taken in this way. And the method of its taking was very simple. That was, just show those documents which are corroborative of your thesis, even though you do have at your disposal a huge number of documents to the contrary. Now all that notwithstanding, in his final brief the Prosecutor wonders in paragraph 573 on the basis of what was it that the witnesses of the -- for the Defence had refreshed their memories? Well, Mr. Moore, the witnesses said it -- said that -- replied to that themselves on the basis of the documents, which the Prosecution had in its possession, when it was taking their statements. Those documents having been previously been disclosed to us, the Defence, but it had no interest to though them to these very same witnesses. And I'm talking about military documents or ECMM documents. This one and only statement on which the Prosecution bases its assertion on the command role of Sljivacanin was taken from Panic almost 15 years after these events. He is now negating it in that part explaining that his memory was refreshed primarily by his being shown a large number of documents and evidence for the first time on the part of the Defence team for Mr. Sljivacanin. Now, who is shying away the establishment of facts in this case? And as a cherry on this top -- on the top of this cake, which is jointly offered us by the Prosecution and Mr. Mrksic's Defence, I should like to say that at the time this only statement of Panic was being taken in which he speaks about de jure Sljivacanin's responsibility, Panic was a potential witness for the Defence of Mr. Mrksic. Then he was very hastily dropped by both the OTP and Mrksic's Defence team. But General Panic appeared before this Tribunal anyhow as a witness for the Defence which wanted and dared find out the truth and inter alia said, and that's at 14420, and I shall say this in his mother tongue, "I hope, I guess that we want the truth to be established here, even in the hardest of moments I went to testify. I've come here regardless of whether I'm a witness for the Prosecution, for the Defence of one or the other party. That is immaterial for me. I'm a person who has participated at certain events. I remember what I remember after so much time has elapsed, but I am one who wants the truth to be established for the sake of all those who worked honourably for the sake of all those who were killed, for the sake of the victims of the war, and because of the lesson which posterity should learn." Should we not have called a witness who utters these words and has so much active knowledge about the event which is actually the subject of this trial to appear before this Tribunal? This is something that actually the Honourable Trial Chamber will tell us in the end through their decision. There is another important detail which one needs to bear in mind in assessing the command function over the evacuation of the hospital. Exhibit 419 is the only written document which makes a reference to the evacuation of the hospital. That is an order on the daily tasks for that day signed by Mrksic. There is no information about the delegation of command authority to anyone, and the tasks are being issued by the commander to all the units, and all the units are in respect of the execution of their tasks including the evacuation of the hospital responsible to the commander, and that was how it was on that day as well. All the reports on the executed tasks in connection with the evacuation of the hospital, the wounded and the sick, as well as the contested evacuation which ended up at Ovcara, were addressed and sent to Mrksic, and we have written in detail about that in our final brief. The Witness Trifunovic who also actually drew up that decision and kept the war log had no knowledge whatsoever about the alleged commanding of the evacuation by Sljivacanin and that is at 8181 in the transcript, but he clearly described, however, what it was that the Chief of Staff did. That's 8009. And that was to follow the implementation of the decisions of the commander and to inform the commander of how his decisions had been carried out in practice. And now let us look at what Panic was doing on that day, the 20th of November. On the basis of the evidence presented, a large bulk of it, at the order of the commander he went to the government session with instructions and thereafter he informed the commander of the outcome of that meeting. Then he went to Ovcara to ascertain how the government decision was being implemented and thereafter informed Commander Mrksic of that. This is the conventional, classical behaviour or conduct, rather, of a Chief of Staff working within the -- his own remit in connection with the commander's decision. So even if the Tribunal accepts the testimony of Gluscevic in regard to the alleged order of Mrksic addressed to the late Bozic, the Court can clearly see from it who was issuing the orders in connection with persons at Ovcara. Mrksic [Realtime transcript read in error "Gluscevic"], according to Gluscevic's words, did not say, "I'm not in charge of that. Vojnovic, go see Sljivacanin. He is the commander. The prisoners are within his competence." No. Throughout that day not a single commanding officer of the OG South, which was the superior command or representatives of the Supreme Command, no one addressed Sljivacanin to inform him of problems or to ask that he take action. They addressed their request to the commander. They reported to him, and they received their orders from him. An intervention in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that -- this is page 27, line 7 in speaking about Mr. Gluscevic, I said Mrksic did not say and then what I quoted would be logical if it was claimed that Sljivacanin was the commander of the evacuation. In a bid to expedite matters I make mistakes. I shall repeat this sentence. Even if the Tribunal should accept Gluscevic's testimony in connection with the alleged order of Mrksic addressed to the late Bozic, and you know what that was, the Court can clearly see from that who is issuing orders in connection with persons in Ovcara, because the commander Mrksic, according to Gluscevic's words, did not say, "I am not competent for that, I'm not in charge for that," but he gave an order that, if need be, they go to Ovcara. So as Gluscevic said, if need be take an armoured battalion and go -- and go to Ovcara. He doesn't say, "I have nothing to do with it. I'm not in charge. Go to Sljivacanin, he's the commander." That's not what he says. The Prosecutor also invokes the testimony of Colonel Vojnovic to the effect that at the meeting on the 19th of November Sljivacanin had stated that he was personally appointed to be in charge of the evacuation. The Defence analysed Vujic's testimony in its brief in detail in respect of that ostensible night meeting in Negoslavci around 1 hour o'clock [as interpreted] after midnight and offered clear proof that this encounter between Sljivacanin and Vujic and his group did not take place at all at that time, but only a meeting around 2000 hours, and on that occasion at that time, Sljivacanin nothing -- said nothing about his alleged command function in respect of the evacuation and Korica's -- and testimony. To conclude this thesis, not a single document does not speak about the command function in the evacuation of the hospital given to Sljivacanin. All the competent witnesses from the very structure of the OG South, the Motorised Brigade, the 80th Brigade, the administration of security, the security administration, the 1st MD, who participated or had direct knowledge about the evacuation of the hospital, and please consult our final brief, the paragraphs being 313 and 32 -- to 325, they are all categorical that on that day Sljivacanin did not issue them any orders whatsoever, or reports on the activities of the participants in the evacuation actually were addressed to the commander of the OG South, and he personally reported -- or rather, informed the superior command on all the activities surrounding the evacuation including the separation and singling out of POWs in his daily report of the 20th of November, 1991, Exhibit 421. Now for the evacuation itself. You have heard two theories on how the evacuation was supposed to take place. Both theories tend to ignore the government session of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as an event that changed the course of the plan itself as well as the evacuation. The Prosecutor claims that both Mrksic and Sljivacanin knew about the arrival of the government members. In relation to Sljivacanin there is absolutely no reference to back that up. Not a single footnote, not a single mention, simply because there is no evidence at all to show that Sljivacanin knew about that. The Prosecutor knows full well, both based on based on witness statements, to what event Sljivacanin was clashing with certain problem members of that government. For example, the minister of the interior Bogunovic and what sort of report he forwarded to the security administration about Prime Minister Hadzic, which is Exhibit 843. Exhibit 843. The Prosecutor knows full well what sort of evidence Goran Hadzic's statement of TV Belgrade was. This is Exhibit 576. And Mr. Vasic knew full well too. They made such an enormous efforts to convince this Trial Chamber, and the Sljivacanin Defence as well, that exhibit was useless, inappropriate, and invalid. And only the verdict will eventually show us if they were right or not. The Sljivacanin Defence submits that this is one of the crucial pieces of evidence in this trial. We submit that this is the document which in the most graphic terms and with no ambiguity whatsoever provides a key to the events that followed. We submit that those events were not planned, were not predictable, nor was Sljivacanin involved in those events in any shape or form. This is a document that smashes into bits the Prosecutor's already paper thin theory on Sljivacanin's involvement in the joint criminal enterprise. What exactly does the Prosecutor do? Mr. Hadzic's statement was introduced by the Prosecutor in the Dokmanovic case when a member of that government stood indicted. In that particular trial, the document appeared to them to be a valid one and, as such, had probative value. Following that, the Prosecutor place this exhibit on their 65 ter list in this trial but decided after all not to tender it into evidence, and they were perfectly within their rights to do that. Then, however, to our great surprise, they opposed asked the Sljivacanin Defence introducing this document as an exhibit. This is a blatant example of how little the Prosecutor cares about the truth. They much prefer simply prosecuting. There must be some sort of primacy of Prosecution over truth at work here, conveniently shoving aside one's own evidence whenever it proves inconvenient. The truth, after all, does not seem to be a primary concern in cases such as these. Why then is this exhibit such a thorn in the side of the Prosecutor and the Mrksic Defence? Simply because it directly corroborates a theory that we have been putting forward from day one of this trial. At this government session in Vukovar, the route of the evacuation was changed and this session was a turning point for the evacuation from the hospital to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Ovcara was not a destination that was envisioned on that day at all. Here we must consider why this exhibit is such a thorn in the side of the Mrksic Defence. You have heard them insist time and time again that the hospital convoy was meant to go to Ovcara because that had been announced in the war log of the 80th Brigade. We defined our own position on this in our final brief. Again, this is a theory that doesn't fit Mr. Moore's purposes, because then Vojnovic and his own brigade are suddenly facing a very inconvenient position. These are certain theories and speculations that other parties to these proceedings have had to face. Not us, however. Let anyone who knows something say whatever it is that they know about Ovcara. Why can't everyone just help and contribute to the healing of these wounds which perhaps can never heal but perhaps can be made to hurt less. Hadzic states for television on that day that, on that day, there was the first government session in Vukovar. It wasn't an informal meeting. It was a government session. The principal decision that was made being that the prisoners were not allowed to leave their territory, and they had apparently reached an agreement with the representatives of the military authorities that the prisoners should stay in the camps around Vukovar. This statement made by Mr. Hadzic is in full collaration [as interpreted] with the evidence given by Vujic and Panic. The notes made by Panic were not written after 2001 and the Mrksic Defence know that full well because they submitted the note to the military court on the 28th of December, 1999, when he gave evidence. This note is fully consistent with Vujic's evidence and what certain persons involved said. It is even consistent with the statement made at page 4562 of Vujic's testimony when he said that Panic had arrived with some sort of notebook or some sort of folder. The Sljivacanin Defence finds it particularly indicative that there was evidence about the threat, or should I say blackmail, made by the minister of the interior, Bogunovic, whom Sljivacanin press charges against over crimes saying that he will, if need be, lie down in front of a tank unless the prisoners were surrendered to them. This is the note made by Mr. Panic. He said that the people would lie down in front of the tanks, not he. Your Honours, it is clear that approval for this government decision could only have been issued by an activity, an order, and for the convoy to be redirected to Ovcara instead of Mitrovica. This is a serious task that you are facing and this is something that you need to establish. Following such information as was shared by Panic with them following which his approval for the send of prisoners, 14307, the meeting soon drew to a close. Unlike Mr. Vasic I'm not surprised by Panic's answers quoted yesterday, "I don't know, I don't know, I don't know." What that shows to my mind is that the decision and what followed was something entirely new to all those who were involved. The Sljivacanin Defence thinks it is entirely reliable to conclude that the buses were in the barracks until the government decision was made. Vujic did not leave the government session and immediately go to the barracks, as Mr. Vasic says. Vujic himself confirms that he stayed in Velepromet for some time after the end of the meeting because he was afraid to leave the room. This is page 4564 of the transcript. And you can see the same thing in that video clip, which is Exhibit 269. But Panic left the room immediately. That's what he says, and that's what Vujic has confirmed. He off to the barracks first thing to inform Colonel Mrksic, and what he finds there are buses. The page is 14321. The buses soon after left the barracks and headed for Ovcara, a camp which Goran Hadzic at the government meeting had referred to as a government camp in the surroundings of Vukovar. The page reference in Panic's evidence is 14313. What else are both the Prosecutor and Mr. Mrksic's Defence saying? They are wondering why the convoy was sent from the hospital to the barracks as a temporary accommodation facility, explaining that the facility did not have a fence, that it was near the notorious location of Velepromet and that it was only logical for the convoy to be sent to Mitrovica straight from the hospital or alternatively to Ovcara as the Mitnica group. They forget that the Vukovar barracks was a facility with a very serious and powerful military structure. This was the location of the forward command post of OG South. They had good and permanent links to Negoslavci. There was a military police company securing the barracks all the time. That's where the command of the 1st Military Police Battalion was. That's where the command post of the 2nd Motorised Battalion was. And the barrack's commander to those were units of the 2nd Motorised Battalion. There was no more fighting on the 20. They forget that on the following day persons from the nearby Velepromet facility were transferred to the barracks. They were offered accommodation and protection until they were eventually taken to Mitrovica. Was there a fence or not? When dealing with a facility like that and the manpower present there this is entirely irrelevant. Where was the fence at Ovcara and who did that fence protect from beating on the 20th of November. An attempt to look for any similarity with the Mitnica location is simply false. We know which area Mitnica belongs to and which area Ovcara belongs to. At Mitnica the people surrendered of their own free will's well as weapons, and at the hospital they didn't. The Mitnica surrender took place in the late afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please be asked to speak up because we can barely make out what he's saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The parameter for the joint criminal enterprise did not occur when these persons were surrendering. It was only after they were put up in the hangar during the night there was no omission in triage itself, as far as the fact was concerned,, and I'm saying this in relation to the hospital that the persons separated were not listed while still at the hospital. They were to be listed before they were surrendered and sent to the Mitrovica prison. But the plan of their evacuation had been changed without Sljivacanin or his associates knowing about it and with no involvement on their part, the aim having been to stay away as far as possible from the anathemised security organs, and from those who so severely criticised the work of that government and their own command. Look at Exhibit 269 in its entirety. It's a video clip. It shows what went on in Velepromet on the 20th of November. You will see at the end of that clip the convoy of buses from the hospital passing the facility; this is the evacuation of the sick wounded and hospital staff. Your Honours, this too shows that the barracks was on the way from the hospital to Sremska Mitrovica. And yes, persons were separated and this convoy with these persons, when a convoy was being set up for the security of these people it was supposed to go to Mitrovica. That's why these people were put up at the barracks and that's why the barracks was the best facility for temporarily accommodating these people. I will now move on to a number of brief observations in relation to certain submissions made by the other parties in their final briefs. It is entirely uncorroborated and contradictory what the Prosecutor says in paragraph 609, namely that Sljivacanin was present at the briefing at the OG South headquarters on the 20th of November when Vojnovic and Mrksic spoke. We presented clear arguments about this in our own brief, paragraphs 711 through 713. Who is saying this? Vojnovic and Vukosavljevic, OTP witnesses, are. Seeing Mrksic, but Sljivacanin is not there, you see. They say they didn't see him. They're crystal clear about that. Vukasinovic is a witness whose evidence is invoked by Mr. Moore because Sljivacanin told him, "I'm off to the meeting." But he's not at the meeting. He's outside his command post, and he doesn't know whether the meeting has already -- had already drawn to a close or not. What leaves us dumbfounded is the fact that in three and a half days of cross-examining Mr. Sljivacanin, the Prosecutor never asks the question. Sljivacanin, in terms of his responsibility under Rule 98, which is something that was so often invoked during our own cross-examinations, they didn't confront Sljivacanin with their own theory, with their own position. No. The Prosecutor never challenged Sljivacanin's evidence as concerns this. The next thing, I will not be commenting specially the Mrksic defence, a proposition on the alleged forgery of Exhibit 422 committed by Panic and Trifunovic. It's down to the Chamber to judge that. But let me draw your attention to Exhibit 425 a report signed by Commander Mrksic on the 22nd of November, signed by him personally, where he says -- where he refers to that forgery and to that decision of the 1st Military District which Mr. Vasic finds to -- to be not credible. Apparently there were raised voices in the conversation that took place between Sljivacanin and Vasiljevic in the 19th of November, but there were none, especially not about the exchange telegram. Karanfilov, whose evidence is referred to by my friend, clearly says that he didn't hear the substance of the conversation between Sljivacanin and Vasiljevic - this is page 15480 - but Witness Karan did hear the substance of their conversation and says that they talked about the desire felt by Karan and Sljivacanin's associates to tape their conversation with Marin Vidic, and Vasiljevic flatly refused. No voices were raised during that conversation, the reference being 15678. Sljivacanin is not exactly a soft speaker and this was amply confirmed by Mr. Moore some days ago when he spoke about his obvious arrogance. The Prosecutor wrongly claims that Sljivacanin didn't testify about the meeting with his subordinate commanders on the 19th of November about the tasks for evacuation. Sljivacanin testified about that in detail, on page 13618, about the tasks he assigned to his subordinate commanders. The Prosecutor also wrongly refers to the testimony of Witness P-012, transcript page 3663, about the fact that allegedly nine persons who were returned from the barracks to the hospital were then returned and sent to Ovcara. Nobody said that, not even that witness. It -- nine persons were not returned, and there are many other testimonies about this fact. Sljivacanin was not in the barracks or at Ovcara on the 20th of November. The Defence of Mr. Sljivacanin has been claiming this from before the pre-trial brief and throughout the entire trial. It seems that the Prosecution did not insist too much on proving this argument. They kept -- they persistently chose not to call of their witnesses who described Sljivacanin in great detail at the hospital, but who also said that they didn't see him at Ovcara or in the barracks. The Prosecution kept waiting for this sole witness of theirs who allegedly saw him in the barracks and at Ovcara and the other witness who saw him only at Ovcara. All other witnesses of the Prosecution, and even of the Defence, did not merit the attention of the Prosecution -- of the Prosecution. They chose not to check this argument with them. I will now continue further about this topic, but perhaps this could be a good time for our break so that I can gain five minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: We will have a break of 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you now have 35 minutes, and then we will hear from the Prosecution whether there is a need for rebuttal. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I started discussing the argument about the alleged presence of Mr. Sljivacanin at the barracks and at Ovcara on the 20th. We discussed this in detail in our written brief concerning the testimony of Witness P-009 and Zlatko Zlogledja. Here, in our closing arguments, I would like to add that we received the greatest support of our argument precisely from the testimony of the OTP witnesses. We didn't fail to ask any of them who described Sljivacanin's appearance at the hospital about their observation in the barracks or at Ovcara concerning Sljivacanin. There were over 15 of such Prosecution witnesses, and we heard from everyone a clear and firm answer, namely that Sljivacanin was not in the barracks and not at Ovcara on the 20th of November. I will next that it was also confirmed by all of Defence witnesses, and to further highlight the neglectful attitude of the Prosecution for this argument of theirs, I will mention the fact that none of those witnesses of the Prosecution were asked in redirect examination and none of the Defence witnesses were asked in cross-examination about this argument of the Prosecution, because the Prosecutor knew what kind of answer he would have received. I would like to remind Mr. Moore of that only because in his final brief he very arbitrarily mentioned that it was only Witness Susic who said that Sljivacanin was not in the barracks. There was a comment there as well that Susic was not in front of the buses throughout the entire time. Let me remind Mr. Moore that -- and I'm not going to mention now the witnesses on the buses. I will only mention those outside of the buses and, namely, there were Panic, Vukasinovic, Maric, and Karanfilov there at different times, and none of them saw Sljivacanin. I will also remind Mr. Moore that he should not forget a great many of his witnesses' documents and videotapes which clearly show where Sljivacanin was at the time when he was allegedly seen at the barracks and at Ovcara. I will remind the Prosecutor that he, the Prosecutor, claims in his final brief in paragraph 565 that Sljivacanin was at the hospital at around 1430 when the convoy set out. Plus we also have an exhibit, 341, which speaks of the fact that convoy left from the hospital at around 1600 hours. And that's precisely the time that the Prosecution witness P-009 claims that Sljivacanin was at Ovcara. Why did we insist so much on establishing as accurately as possible the time-frame of Sljivacanin's alleged presence in the barracks and at Ovcara? Witness P-009 was very vague when he -- when it came to his memory and earlier statements. Everything became physically impossible in those statements, or perhaps there were more than one Sljivacanin in Vukovar or even Sljivacanin was an epitome of the entire JNA in Vukovar. Despite such obvious media bias about his role in Vukovar events, almost all witnesses of the Prosecution were unequivocal; namely, they did not see Sljivacanin either at the barracks or at Ovcara. This document, the folder provided by Mr. Moore two days ago, with quoted words of witnesses about Sljivacanin is an excellent example of the work of Prosecution and a further support of my position. Mr. Moore brilliantly showed his approach to the final brief and closing arguments. Take out just what suits you and pretend that nothing else exists, as though all of us here in this courtroom did not spend a year and a half together listening to the testimonies. However, one cannot get around the fact that all of those witnesses who described Sljivacanin at the hospital in such great detail did not see Sljivacanin either at the barracks or at Ovcara, and he is such a man, as Witness Berghofer put it and Mr. Moore quoted it, that one can recognise him from a distance of one kilometre. Your Honours, this will be a difficult and thankless task for you to compare all of these testimonies at the hospital. Some of the witnesses said that Sljivacanin did not address them. Some claim the opposite. Some said that he issued orders. Some didn't hear those orders. Some said that he went outside of the bus area. Some say that he didn't. Some say that he ordered the buses to set out. The others claim that it wasn't him. However, it is undisputable that Sljivacanin was at the hospital on the 20th in the morning and also in the afternoon hours. What did Mr. Sljivacanin actually do when it comes to the evacuation of the hospital? He participated together with the security organs, doctors, and hospital staff, despite of how difficult it is to some of them to acknowledge it now. He worked with them in order to ensure all the necessary conditions for evacuation of the wounded and the sick, and the separation or triage of the persons who had to be separated. Even though this doesn't suit Mr. Moore, Sljivacanin did the work he had to do within his duties, his competence, together with the officers of the security organs of the 1st Military District and security administration. He had to. He was supposed to act in accordance with the order of the superior command. There are two documents proving this and you heard about that Exhibit 316 and 333. They speak clearly about the fact that on the 19th of November, Pavkovic did not give the consent for the wounded members of Croatian forces to be evacuated. Not only those who were hiding and disguising but also Croatian fighters who were wounded. On the 20th of November in the morning, Colonel Pavkovic told the representatives of the ECMM that there was a definitive - I stress definitive - order of General Raseta that wound members of the Croatian forces who were at the hospital could not be evacuated. This is Exhibit 333. And what was the task of security organs now that we have all this information? That they should not allow those who Mr. Moore calls former town defenders to be evacuated. Why does the Prosecutor wish to stress as contentious the fact that in one part of that work the security organs used both local residents and TO members in order to gain information? Let me just stress that the Prosecution expert Mr. Pringle, in paragraph 74 of Exhibit 600, said that everything that Mr. Sljivacanin did was fully legitimate. Nothing was done covertly in this operation. Quite the contrary. The representatives of the European mission and journalists were told by Sljivacanin upon their arrival at the hospital that those people had been separated and taken to the prison. Please look at Exhibit 837 and 840, and please look at exhibits invoked by the Prosecutor in their paragraph 225 of the final brief. Yes, Mr. Moore, Sljivacanin did say to the representatives of the European Monitoring Mission that those people had been separated and taken to prison. Mr. Moore, did you ask your witnesses, Kypr and Schou, who confirmed this fact, did they inquire about where these people had been taken? Did they ask to go and write down their names? No, you didn't ask them that. However, Sljivacanin told them clearly about this fact. Just how much did you distance yourself by your position in paragraph 225 from the participation of Sljivacanin in the joint criminal enterprise? The Prosecutor particularly highlights the civilian status of victims at Ovcara, and perhaps now I'll touch upon the question that will be later dealt on with the -- by the Trial Chamber. Now I will refer to the status of victims themselves. First of all, I wish to say that I fully support the final brief of the Defence of Mr. Radic, paragraph 71 to 128. They spoke in detail about this fact. We know very well just how much Mrs. Tapuskovic and Ms. Dokmanovic analysed this issue, especially Mrs. Tapuskovic. I have to mention the following: The documents and testimonies clearly speak of the status of the victims. The following is also important: Out of 200 bodies exhumed from the grave at Ovcara, eight were never identified. Out of 192 remaining bodies, for some reason the Prosecutor never included two persons in the annex of the indictment. Out of 190 remaining bodies, four families never accepted the results of the identification, and these people are still listed as missing. Finally, out of 186 bodies, the Defence teams conducted a very detailed comparative analysis of the documents provided by the Prosecution. 452, Exhibit 452, Strinovic; Exhibit 544, which is Grujic's testimony; then the documents provided by Dr. Bosanac, Exhibits 345 and 346, as well as autopsy records, Exhibit 462. These documents, unfortunately I'm speaking of dry facts here own though this involves individual human lives, show us that among the exhumed there are at least 155 members, reported members, of Croatian armed paramilitary formations, many of whom had nothing to do at the hospital, especially if we take into account the fact that they disguised themselves. For example, record OVC 181 indicates that the number is even higher. I definitely do not wish to question the pain of the families or to minimise the tragedy at Ovcara. I also do not wish to deny the status of the wounded combatants who are entitled to protection under international standards. However, this protection does not prevent the JNA from separating those persons whose status is disputed at that point in time. Even Borsinger, the representative of the ICRC, in his talk with Pavkovic, Exhibit 335 and 336, says: "The role of the Red Cross is not to help the fighters to disguise and to -- civilians and be evacuated from the hospital." Then several seconds later, once again Borsinger says, "I will never prevent you from doing your job." He says that to Colonel Pavkovic. Please look at that exhibit. In the interests of justice, we have to underline what is necessary in establishing material facts of a crime, that we cannot say that the majority of the victims here were civilians and had the status of civilians. This is based first and foremost on the facts provided by the families of the victims as well as by the administration of the Vukovar Hospital and autopsy reports. Now I'm going to move on to a key issue in this trial on which you will have to render your final judgement, honourable Tribunal, for our benefit, and that is who was it and at whose orders that actually withdrew the security unit of the 80th Motorised Brigade from Ovcara and which is very important as a fact for our defence, whether evidence, whether proof has been offered that Sljivacanin had anything to do with that obviously misguided decision. You have heard and read two assertions. According to Mr. Moore it was only Karanfilov who would have transmitted that order which could -- then could have only been issued by Mrksic, but it is logical, says he, there is no other proof in the Prosecutor's rationale except that it is logical that that went through Sljivacanin. According to Mr. Vasic, that was also what Karanfilov did. According to that contingent, both Panic and Sljivacanin waited for Mrksic to leave for Belgrade because they knew that he, Mrksic, would never have allowed it so that they transmitted an order to Razmanovic [phoen] to withdraw via Karanfilov. The objective was to divert attention by this crime from the Croatian crime in Gospic and for General Vasiljevic to get his captured collaborators from the Labrador Operation and then, in return, Croatia international recognition. Distinguished Bench, as I have indicated in the beginning, your task here is not to establish a criminal liability for so grave a crime on the basis of logic, imagination, or construction, but on the basis of proof and facts, on the basis of evidence to which you shall lend credence or not. That is the basis of your assessment and your conclusion and ultimately the mandate entrusted to you by the international community. In its final brief the Defence team of Mr. Sljivacanin has analysed in detail the evidence which is solely and exclusively of the essence for your conclusions, and the evidence, primarily Exhibit 371, clearly states that the security unit assigned to the hangar at -- was assigned to the hangar at 16 hours on the 20th by Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, the only person who could legitimately do so, and also then that security unit was withdrawn at 2230 hours by the only person who could legitimately do so, the one who had ordered it and who was able to retract his decision. And it was only Commander Vojnovic who could issue such an order to his unit and none other. In JNA there existed the principle of singleness of command, and Vojnovic, too, clearly testified that he had sent Vukosavljevic to relay his order to Vezmarovic, and Vukosavljevic also went to Ovcara. He did not rule out the possibility that he had relayed that order to Vezmarovic. That is at 8803 in the transcript. And Vezmarovic himself testified that perhaps Vukosavljevic had relayed to order to him. That's 8589 in the transcript. And I should like to underline Vukosavljevic testified that after that he informed the person who had issued him the order, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, and that's at page 8805. I should also like to know that Vukosavljevic himself expressed doubts when he heard the assertion about the alleged appearance of Karanfilov for the first time, and that was in 2003. And, as he put it, it was some sort of a variant of the description of the incident of the event that Vezmarovic talked about, and that's at 8812. That's logical, as my learned colleague Mr. Moore would put it, for Vukosavljevic to have thought that because there, at Ovcara, he could see Karanfilov nowhere. These are facts, and these are evidentiary assertions that both Mr. Moore and Mr. Vasic are steering clear off. Doubtlessly Vojnovic sent Vukosavljevic to relay the order to Captain Vezmarovic to withdraw his unit. It is indubitable that Vukosavljevic and Vezmarovic returned alone together and informed Vojnovic thereof, and that was entered in the war log of the 80th Brigade. That evening, no one at all noted in the war log that the withdrawal had been executed outside the chain of command, and it is quite clear that also on the 18 -- that on the 18th of November as well Karanfilov had no command authority whatsoever over Vezmarovic. You can consult the testimonies of Vojnovic, Mr. Moore's favourite witness, on page 9085. He did not order that to Vezmarovic. And then look at Danilovic's statement, and who is the favourite witness of the Defence of Mr. Mrksic, and that's at transcript 12367. The commander of the camp, Danilovic, claims it was impossible for the command of the military police to receive any orders without him being involved, but Karanfilov needed to be discredited as much as possible in order to obfuscate the so-clear path to the truth. That is why his earlier statements were used in order to disrupt what he had claimed from the -- from his first statement and he has given -- he gave eight of them. On the day Karanfilov was not at Ovcara and Vasiljevic was not at Negoslavci. And Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic were not at the examination, the interrogation in Negoslavci on the 20th of November, but on the 19th of November, and you have heard a number of testimonies and they're all consistent in this regard. In fact, Vesna Bosanac herself at 688, and Karan, that is 15557, and Sljivacanin, 13596, and Karanfilov, at 15418, all say the same thing. And Karanfilov who was -- who they wanted so much to mix up the dates clearly described how after eight statements he was shown for the first time during the proofing for this testimony the necessary documentation, video clips, and documents, and that is at transcript 154358, of so many investigators all throughout these 15 years, no one wished, and they were able to, to show the -- the witness any document. It seems that this was all in pursuit of the objective that I've already referred to. And then when the entire sequence of events from the adoption of the decision on the setting up of the security unit up to their withdrawal clearly and only functioned in compliance with rules and regulations upon the principles of unity of command; according to precise chain of command, that chain needed to be severed and another one made up. And then, of course, the command authority of Karanfilov needed to be established, which is impossible on the basis of regulations, and also impossible on the quite clear testimonies of Vojnovic and Danilovic. So Karanfilov did not have command powers at -- in any single moment and Vezmarovic could not nor dared act according to his alleged orders. No. Vezmarovic exclusively and solely acted according to the decisions of the person who issued him the order according to the regulations and in actual practice to come to Ovcara and to then withdraw from Ovcara, and that was Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. That is what we heard from him. The evidence is inexorable. Sljivacanin has nothing whatsoever to do with that decision nor has a single piece of evidence been presented that would not only be beyond any doubt but associate Sljivacanin with that decision in any way. I will now draw your attention to several contentions of the OTP regarding the JCE. Not so much from a legal aspect, which, actually, Mr. Moore did not explore that much, but just some factual underpinnings of his contention. What Mr. Moore has offered us is stated in paragraph 362, in which he adds new members of the JCE by name and surname. All those who actually are adulterated by their testimonies, his contention, as it were, to the effect that in that enterprise, the pursuit of a joint plan, there also had to be the arch scoundrel, the compliment, actually, that Mr. Moore paid to the witness, Vukasinovic. And that was a witness which according to accounts -- at whom, according to accounts, TO members had pointed their guns three times that day and who on arrival at the hangar managed to personally expel all those persons from the hangar. Vojnovic, who is -- who also opposes and takes on those territorials is, according to the Prosecutor, a hero. And Vukasinovic who does the same is, in his book, a member of the JCE, with a number of insults into the bargain. It is obvious that Panic's and Karanfilov's testimony do not soothe the OTP and we have seen why; that is why they need to be anathemised. Both Mr. Moore and Mr. Vasic claim that organs of security could have discharged duties outside their remits, and they invoke Exhibit 374 on the appointment of Vukasinovic as town commander to support that. They seem to forget what actually happened, what was in Negoslavci. Let me remind them. It was the command post of the Guards Brigade and of the command post of the OG South. I should like to remind them also of the fact that one of the basic tasks from the remit of the OB and -- is the organisation of the security of the command. According to Article 7 of the rules of service of the OB and there cannot be a more suitable commanding officer to control and organise security than the actual commanding officer of the OB unit. The appointment of Vukasinovic of town commander was Commander Mrksic's decision within the remit of OB and I think beyond it.
