If it was outside his ambit, as my learned colleague asserts, then a written decision on it only demonstrates what kind of a form is necessary to issue orders to an officer of security outside his remit. I shall just say a few words about the proposed sentence. In our brief we didn't see anything about extenuating or aggravating circumstances, and we now consider that to be deeply on a collision course with our proposal, but we did deal with a part which refers to the character of Mr. Sljivacanin. That's in paragraphs 892 to 908. That person, his character, his person of a professional soldier, his conduct in war, his desire for the war operations to stop, his human care for civilians, not only as a human being but -- not only as an officer but as a human being, but also his attitude when it came to the deaths of his soldiers, ordinary troops, but we can also say observed from the aspect of the JNA, heroes, is something that you must bear in mind to establish -- in establishing his liability. I can only wonder whether the Prosecutor is proposing this sentence due to -- to his impotence to impress the Court with his proof. Is it only on formalism that he bases his perception of Sljivacanin's liability when he proposes this sentence? Sljivacanin decided to take the stand first in his evidentiary procedure. During the trial he wished to actively contribute to the efficiency of the proceedings, also when he was in hospital for treatment. Your Honours, we cannot say whether we have been helpful to you in establishing the truth. We did our best in professional terms, and we have also followed clear instructions from Mr. Sljivacanin. We did not speculate or toy around with evidence. We tried to bring such witnesses before the Trial Chamber as could provide reliable answers to many questions, as were raised throughout this trial. This trial has gone on for a year and a half. What we now leave behind us are times filled with stories of evil, pain, crime, and wounds that cannot heal. It is the truth that must crush all prejudice accumulated over the years among the public. One of the greatest prejudices is the role purportedly played by Sljivacanin in Vukovar. An executioner, a Chetnik, a Commie, and an arrogant liar. Sljivacanin was in no way involved in this crime and in no shape or form did he have any share in this or in the subsequent responsibility. Sljivacanin's sole crime was that he had faith in a country, in a flag, and in an oath. It is because of this faith, it is for the sake of him and everybody else who had had the same faith, that you must crush prejudice by establishing the truth. A part of that truth is your own verdict by which you will establish that Veselin Sljivancanin is not guilty of the crimes that were committed at Ovcara. Your Honours, this is the end of my closing argument. I would like to use up another minute or two to say this: I would like to express my gratitude, and I think I'm speaking on behalf of all three Defence teams, to all those who have contributed to this trial running as smoothly as it has. We wish to thank the Detention Unit, who showed particular care and affection for our clients when their health was at stake. I also wish to thank the interpreters, and I wish to thank them for their work today. I wish to thank the Victims and Witnesses Protection Unit in a very special way. I also wish to thank my own team as well as all the witnesses who appeared on behalf of Mr. Sljivacanin, raising no objection whatsoever and having no regard to their own personal interest and benefit. I wish to thank them all. Finally, I wish to thank the Chamber for giving me an opportunity to appear before this Court, which has been a great honour for me. As my learned friend Mr. Borovic has said, we have tried here to cross swords with the OTP, and I believe that a trace will remain of our legal efforts here in the history of international law. Some of the experiences that we have had throughout our time here will no doubt prove of value back in our own countries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now the question is, will there be argument in rebuttal and in rejoinder. Mr. Moore. The answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The answer is in the following way: May I endorse my learned friend's thanks to all parties and may I additionally thank the Defence for the courtesy to which they have applied -- applied to us through this trial. With regard to the rebuttal matter, I will not deal with any issues that have been raised except the point that Your Honour has already mentioned by way of the definition of "civilian."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Then I think we can proceed to that point now. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I didn't know whether Your Honour wished to see whether the defendants had anything to say prior to this or for subsequent -- or subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: We were thinking of having that at the very end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. The Court has posed an interesting question which has exercised many minds. The question clearly concerns the point of law, and if I may just read again into the record the question that Your Honour has posed. "Is the question whether the victims of a crime against humanity where civilians are not relevant to the applicability of Article 5. In other words, is the general condition of the civilian status of the targeted population that is required for a chapeau requirement identical to the condition of the civilian status of the victims of the underlying crime?" I hope I read it correctly. May I deal with it in this way: The Trial Chamber has asked us whether Article 5 requires proof that the victims of the underlying crimes were civilians and whether the civilian status requirement in the chapeau of Article 5 is identical to that required for the victims of the underlying crimes. May I begin by giving a brief summary of our answer, and then I hopefully will explain it in a little more detail and address the Tribunal's existing case law on that matter. There will be two parts to my answer. The first is this: That all of the victims of the crimes pleaded under Article 5 in the present case qualify as civilians under Article 5. They were either persons who had never participated in hostilities, or they were persons who were hors de combat, and so were no longer participating in hostilities. Our position is that the scope of protection afforded by Article 5 is broad and broad enough to encompass both of these categories of persons. The second aspect of my reply is as follows: Because your question also appears to raise an issue that goes beyond the facts of the present case, namely can victims of crimes against humanity include those who participate in hostilities, for example, combatants. The answer to this hypothetical question is that such persons could be considered as victims of a crime against humanity even though they do not qualify as civilians by definition. This would be so in the circumstances where they are targeted in a manner that is unlawful under IHL. However, if combatants are targeted in a manner that is lawful under IHL, then clearly no crime has been committed and quite simply the matter ceases there. May I just move on and deal with the -- the victim of an Article 5 crime and the definition of civilian under Article 5. As I've already indicated in brief outline the definition of "civilian" under Article 5 of the Statute includes all persons who are not participants hostilities. In other words, a civilian under Article 5 is anyone who is not the lawful object of attack under IHL. This includes persons who are hors de combat, for example, through sickness or through being detained by an opposing party. In this way the term "civilian" under Article 5 does not have an identical meaning to the term "civilian" in Additional Protocol I regulating international armed conflicts in Additional Protocol I persons who are classified as hors de combat are a separate category of analysis and are not subsumed in the term "civilian." However, under IHL, persons hors de combat and civilians are nevertheless on the same footing. They are accorded substantially similar protections. More significantly or most significantly, neither category of persons can be the object of attack, only combatants participating in the hostilities can be the object of an attack. So it is the principle of distinction between combatants and non-combatants which is the key under IHL regardless of the labels used. This is reflected in the IHL principles regulating internal armed conflict. For example, in Common Article 3 and Additional Protocol II, the only distinction drawn is between persons taking no active part in hostilities or persons who do not take a direct part or who have ceased to take part in hostilities, and those who do take part in hostilities. Common Article 3 expressly places persons hors de combat in the category of persons who take no active part in the hostilities and who may not be attacked. In our commission, the reference to civilians in Article 5 is intended to reflect the same distinction as set out in Common Article 3. The protection stemming from the civilian status extends to anyone not taking an active or a direct part in hostilities, including persons who are hors de combat. The operation of IHL as lex specialis does not, in our submission, prevent such a conclusion. It does not require that the term "civilian" in Article 5 be given precisely the same definition as under IHL, regulating international armed conflicts consistent with the Blaskic appeal judgement at paragraph 110. The definition of civilian under IHL is relevant in defining that term under Article 5. However, there is nothing to mandate that the terms must be defined in identical terms. What is required is that the term "civilian" in Article 5 cannot be interpreted in a manner that undermines IHL. In particular, the term "civilian" under Article 5 cannot be defined to include persons who are lawful objects of attack under IHL. That, however, does not prevent the approach that we submit is appropriate here, that is based on the distinction drawn in IHL itself between persons who do not take part in hostilities it and so may not be attacked and those who do, who may legitimately be attacked. The definition of civilian under Article 5 that we advocate is supported by a number of Tribunal authorities; for example, the Rule of 61 decision in this case, which held that persons hors de combat may fall within the definition of civilians under Article 5. The Chamber on that occasion reviewed the indictment pursuant to Article 61 -- to Rule 61, held that although according to the terms of Article 5 of the Statute of this Tribunal, the combatants in the traditional sense of the term cannot be victims of a crime against humanity. This does not apply to individuals who at one particular point in time carried out acts of resistance. May I refer the Bench to paragraph 29 of that decision. Secondary, may I direct Your Honours' attention to the Akayesu trial judgement in paragraph 582. There it held that members of the civilian population are people who are not taking any active part in the hostilities, including members of the armed force who lay down their arms and those persons placed hors de combat. The Trial Chamber in that case noted in a footnote that this definition assimilates the definition of civilian with the categories of persons protected by Common Article 3. The Tadic trial judgement there, the Trial Chamber asked which individuals could be considered as civilians for the purposes of Article 5. After surveying a number of sources, the Trial Chamber concluded that a wide definition of civilian population, as supported by these sources, is justified. Thus the presence of those actively involved in the conflict should not prevent the characterisation of a population as civilian and those actively involved in a resistance movement can qualify as victims of crimes against humanity. And in that it also referred to the Mrksic rule where it actually used it as an authority in the following way: Although crimes against humanity must target a civilian population, individuals who at one point in time performed acts of resistance may in certain circumstances be victims of crimes against humanity. In the context of that case, patients in a hospital, either civilians or resistance fighters who had laid down their arms were considered crimes against humanity. Of course that is this case. Finally, may I refer Your Honours to a case decided by this very Trial Chamber. That was the Limaj trial judgement. In that case Your Honours held in paragraph 186 when discussing the term "civilian population," in Article 5 that, and I quote: "The presence within a population of members of resistance armed groups or former combatants who have laid down their arms does not as such alter its civilian nature." Importantly, Your Honours went on to observe, "as a result, the definition of a civilian is expansive, and includes individuals who at one time performed acts of resistance, as well as persons hors de combat when the crime was committed. May I deal then, please, with the Blaskic appeal judgement. Would Your Honour wish me to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The Blaskic appeal judgement does not preclude this approach. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber dealt with the issue of who may constitute a civilians for the purpose of Article 5. Our submission is that the Blaskic appeal judgement does not preclude the approach we advocate -- or advocate and which is reflected in the case law that we have cited. The Appeals Chamber focused on the following comment made by the Blaskic Trial Chamber, and I quote: "It also follows that the specific situation of the victim at the moment the crimes were committed, rather than his status, must be taken into account in -- in determining his standing as a civilian." That's at paragraphs 109, 108, and 114. The Appeals Chamber was of the view or expressed the view that this statement may be misleading. The Appeals Chamber then extracted a passage from the ICRC commentary to Protocol I, which dispels the notion that there is a category of part-time combatant status, that a person could be considered a combatant by day and a peaceful civilian by night. The key point is that if that person is targeted at night, when the person was no longer engaged in combat, this does not mean that the individual is no longer a combatant and has immunity from attack. Under IHL a person who is not considered as a person who is no longer actively participating in hostilities just because at a given point in time he is not engaged in combat. For that reason, the Appeals Chamber concluded that the specific situation of the victim at the time the crimes were committed may not be determinative of his civilian or non-civilian status. We submit that is correct. Under IHL, a person who is a combatant but who happens not to be engaged in combat at a particular moment in time, may still be lawfully attacked. However, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber did not focus on the situation that we are concerned about in this case. For that reason, the Blaskic case is distinguishable, in our submission. The hors de combat victims in the present case were no longer participating in any hostilities at all for the time that they had that status, and we submit that this is confirmed by the language of Article 3. Under IHL, they could not be the lawful object of attack, and that is the key distinction and is the basis for our submission that the Blaskic appeal judgement does not preclude extending the term "civilian" to encompass persons who would be considered hors de combat. May I pose then the following question? It's simply this: Can combatants be considered as victims of Article 5 crimes? The broader issue raised by Your Honours' question whether persons participating in the hostilities could ever be considered as victim of Article 5 crimes does not, as I say, arise on the facts of this case. However, we would submit that the combatants can be considered victims of a crime against humanity if they are victimised in a way that is unlawful under IHL. IHL's status as lex specialis imposes limitations on the extent to which combatants can be considered victims of the Article 5 crimes. In particular, the death of a person in lawful combat activity under IHL logically could not become unlawful and a crime against humanity under Article 5. Beyond this kind of scenario, however, it is possible that a combatant who is targeted in a way that is unlawful under IHL could be counted among the victims of a crime against humanity. There are various authorities which I can refer to in relation to the Supreme Court of Germany in the British occupied zone following World War II entered convictions for crimes against humanity in at least three instances where the victims were regular soldiers, and in one of those cases the judgement concluded that, "whoever notes the expressly emphasised character of the instances and classes of instance mentioned there cannot come to the conclusion that action between soldiers may not constitute crimes against humanity." So I respectfully repeat and stress that this question does not arise on the facts of this case since, as we have already submitted, the victims here were hors de combat and no longer participating in the hostilities. We have endeavoured to deal with the matter as expeditiously and as neatly as we can. If, however, and it is a complex matter and I think everyone understands that, if the Court would wish any further explanation or expansion of our position, we would be willing and happy to do so in written form with that will assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Now we will hear the submissions for the Defence. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you. I will try to respond also to the question raised by the Chamber as well as to the question raised by Mr. Moore. I would like to say something before I start and before I provide an answer to that question. All three of our Defence teams have made clear our positions on the existence or non-existence of essential elements for the application of Article 5 of the Tribunal's Statute. We think the elements have not been met to prove that an attack like that was carried out against the JNA, an attack against civilians at the period of time covered by indictment. I would like to focus on something that my learned friend Mr. Moore has said in his own closing argument about this. It's about Exhibit 312 and Exhibit 305. This is an exhibit which he refers to as the Babska declaration. We can see that on page 663 of the transcript, the exhibit was introduced through Witness Kypr. Kypr didn't know where the exhibit came from. It wasn't something that he obtained himself. The Defence at the time raised doubts as to the authenticity of the document purportedly showing that there was an ultimatum given to the civilian population, to the citizens of Babska to hand over their weapons lest they were flattened, as this -- or razed to the ground, as this handwritten document appears to suggest. Its authenticity was never proved. The other exhibit I'm talking about is 312. Again, this is about the attack against civilians. It was introduced through Witness Kypr. This was a document that was drafted during The Hague Conference, and the Defence claims that it was a form of political pressure put on the Yugoslav authorities. The transcript reference is 6702 through 6704. We see there clearly that Kypr knows nothing about who produced that document. As to the most important portion of this document, which is something especially raised by my learned friend, the attack against civilians, he only seems to know about Lovas, and that's the only place he mentions, and we do know for a fact that there was no attack by the JNA in Lovas. What occurred there was people being killed as a result of actions taken by a group led by the self-styled commander, Ljuban Devetak. So that is the premise that I wish to establish before I launch into my principal subject, which is attacks against civilians. Unlike my learned friend, the Defence believes that in order to be able to apply Article 5, victims need to be civilians, and this is something that has been established in the Kunarac sentence and the Krnojelac sentence, in previous trials before this Tribunal. We believe there is no dilemma at all about that. What my learned friend is pleading today, we believe, cannot be applied in relation to Article 5. There are other norms of international humanitarian law addressing the issue. It is quite clear that we have a final sentence, a final ruling here, the sentence in the Blaskic case which clearly defines and accepts a comment made by the Red Cross, in fact, a comment about how the category of civilians should be defined. Bearing in this mind, we can say that the provisions of Article 30 of the Additional Protocol of the Geneva Conventions defined the status of civilians. This is a negative definition of what is envisaged under Article 4(A), items 1, 2, 3 and 6 of the Geneva Conventions and Article 43 of the first Protocol. This encompasses all the persons who were taken out of the hospital on the morning of the 20th of November. That is what the Defence teams are saying. We believe there were no civilians among those people. All those who on the morning of the 20th of November were taken away were combatants. We do agree, however, that their civilian status cannot be challenged if we have a group of civilians their civilian status cannot be challenged just because there happens to be the occasional fighter among them. But we do believe that in this group there were people who had not laid down their weapons, and there was not a civilian majority in this group. This is clearly demonstrated by what we have presented as a conclusion after questioning the members of the committee for missing persons, Croatia's committee for missing persons. We looked through documents that they had been working on for years, and we saw what the figure regarding the active fighters was. I think about 155. I think that's what my learned friend has said. We also need to bear in mind the fact that in addition to the active fighters belonging to the National Guards Corps and the MUP, there was an involvement also by the volunteers and the civilian protection. In my closing argument, I pointed out that most of its members were involved, most citizens of Vukovar, especially after the mobilisation had taken effect. That is precisely this provision defining what sort of group can be considered as a civilian group and what sort of group can be considered combatants stems from the terms provided by the International Red Cross. At page 515, paragraph 1676, it says that no group taking part in combat or carrying weapons can be considered as a civilian group. The status of such a group and their protection can only be ensured in -- in the case of wounding under the first and second Geneva Conventions and when taking prisoners under the provisions of the third Geneva Conventions, and not under the provisions Article 5 of the Statute granting protection only to a group of civilians that is attacked. What is essential here is that the group raised in the indictment is a group that was separated from all the wounded patients or any other civilians who had either been transferred to Velepromet or were hospital staff and left on the convoy that left Vukovar on the 20th at half past 3.00. So this group that was kept there in the morning was made up of those persons alone who had been a party to the hostilities, had been involved in the hostilities. They were combatants; therefore, their status could not additionally have been changed into that of civilians as Mr. Moore seems to have pleaded. Therefore, my position is that, as concerns any crime under Article 5 of the Statute, victims must have a civilian status. The conclusion therefore is the victims in this case the victims refer to in the indictment had no such status. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall just add to what colleague Vasic has said on our joint behalves. As regards the status of victims referred to by the OTP in their final briefs, they pointed that these were the sick and the wounded and under the first Geneva Convention applied and the corresponding provisions of Additional Protocols 1 and 2 thereto, which refer to the sick and wounded; however, in the indictment, I believe I said so yesterday, the persons from the hospital are defined as detainees, patients, and captured persons. And then the OTP also in another spot defines them as evacuees. Today we heard that all the persons who ceased participating in the hostilities, including combatants who had lay their arms, could acquire the status of a civilian person, and they were the victims of a crime. If we speak about specific matters we know from the evidence that was presented when it refers -- in so much as it refers to the combatants who lay their arms, that does not apply to this case. The combatants who were found in the Vukovar hospital had not laid down their arms. It was the Mitnica group that had done so and therefore it acquired the status which entitles it to protection under the Geneva Convention. I believe that this is a matter of substance. I'm not going to go into explaining the correlation between the objectives of assaults on this or that group of civilian population. This is something, it has to be a primary objective, as we know, but that would already be an assessment of evidence. So we do have a joint position on the civilian status of victims which is that in this case they were not civilians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly with the reservation that during these two days I did not focus much on your question, but we of course discussed it and I fully subscribe to Mr. Vasic's and Mr. Borovic's words. I should like to say that in respect of the category of civilian population, we wrote about that in paragraph 767 to 774 of our brief and that is how we perceive civilian population as a necessary condition for Article 5 of the Statute. Let me just add that I oppose Mr. Moore's thesis that the verdict in the Brdjanin -- sorry, in the Blaskic case is not relevant to our case. I believe that it is exceptionally relevant, and in terms of our concrete case, we know that that is a second instance and final verdict. As regards the civilian or non-civilian status, we actually invoked that judgement in both our pre-trial and final briefs, and I'm going to read it and.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 114 of the second instance of the appellate jurisdiction in the Blaskic case, the Appellate Chamber's conclusion says: "Because of that, the specific situation of the victim in the moment of the commission of the crime does not necessarily determine its civilian versus not civilian status. If he is indeed a member of an armed organisation, the fact that he is unarmed or does not participate in combat at the time of the commission of the crime does not give him, does not accord him civilian status." To me this is it. This is the end of the discussion. There is no dilemma at all for a legal conclusion which for us here in this courtroom is the source of law. As Mr. Borovic says -- said, this is not people -- persons who had laid down their arms but these are and the assilerate [as interpreted] that, persons who had concealed their weapons of course that is up to the procedure of evidence proving but this is -- this position from the Blaskic judgement is extremely important and relevant; that is why we invoked it in both our briefs. These victims who did not have their arms a that moment were not therefore civilians according to that judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I'm looking at the time. At this moment in time we -- the Trial Chamber has been told that both Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivacanin want to address the Trial Chamber. I suggest that we have a break and that we resume and then the parties will let us know. I'm sorry. So we could still go for 45 minutes. Can -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: So does Mr. Mrksic want to address the Court? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you for giving me an opportunity to address the Court at the end of this trial. I have every confidence in your work. I have seen you follow the trial closely, and I trust that you will bring a just verdict. I have been listening to the lawyers as well. There have been certain disagreements. I would like to say a couple of words. I'm not going to the merits of the case, of course, but I want to say something about some of the things that the Prosecutor said yesterday. They started their closing argument by putting forward a theory to the effect that I was creating officers in the Guards Brigade who were brutal, who in terms of their demeanour and behaviour caused fear among other people, fear and a climate of intolerance. I do wish to say one thing. It is generally known what sort of officers are required for any Guards Unit, and I believe the same applies to the unit that Mr. Moore served in himself in England. We did everything within our power for our officers to be athletic, cultured, clean-shaven, nice looking, and clear in their approach. I said this to Mr. Vance. He was quite satisfied at the time. I don't know how the theory came about that I struck anyone at all as an arrogant - I'm not sure exactly what they said - an arrogant person, someone to be feared. Mr. Moore said that, and later he concluded based on this that there was some sort of a joint criminal enterprise. What I'm trying say is this: No such people could remain in the Guards Brigade. No such people could have ever become members of the Guards Brigade. No brutality was tolerated, to other soldiers or indeed to their wives even. If their wives came over and complained about these soldiers, I would have had them transferred. Each of our officers had to be well-liked, well-loved by all other officers. That's what our officers were like, and that's why in combat a lot of our officers were killed in a bid to protect their own soldiers. If any of our officers at all ever said anything about any other ethnicity, statements that weren't in the spirit of the principles of the Guards Brigade, these soldiers had to be transferred. If anyone at all said they would have wronged any other ethnicity in any way, they would never have been taken on by the Guards Brigade. We built up our relationships on brotherhood and unity, on our traditions dating back to a time when Comrade Tito was still alive, and even earlier traditions. Any stories saying that we wanted to create a joint criminal enterprise and expel the Croats are stories that I can't accept. My officers never could possibly have conceived of anything like that, and that is why I refute this. I have many questions myself why certain things happened in a certain way. Sometimes things were unclear. When the fighting started I didn't understand myself why I had to remain in Vukovar all the time. Mr. Moore was right when he said that it was a new Stalingrad. Who knows in whose interest this was? I had the Bogdanovci three metres behind me in my own combat disposition. I was shown that image of the destruction of Vukovar 15 years later. I realise who this served, towns and cities are laid siege to and sometimes they just fall. There's no need to destroy towns and cities. However, these were political and military decisions and our job was to carry them out. Cui bono, who stood to profit from this? This is something I leave to historians, and I think analysts on Croatian TV are talking about this publicly. Why were the civilians returned to Vukovar? In order to make the defenders as firm, as strong as possible, and in order for the Vukovar defenders to crush and defeat the very spearhead of the JNA, the Guards Brigade. The divisions and other brigades were scattered all over Srem. By the time we arrived in Vukovar there were tanks but no soldiers, artillery weapons but no soldiers, armies abandoning their positions, deserting, that sort of thing. There was chaos all over the place. People were coming up with ideas like, "Stop. Give it up." But still we were the Guards Brigade. We got our mission, and we would complete our mission. We would see to it that our mission was completed. When we faced a crisis when our reservists abandoned us, we still remained. We did our best. We fought hard. We tried to restore order and discipline even under those conditions, and we were to some extent successful. As long as the fighting was still going on, we had no trouble at all. They won't surrender. Marin Vidic calls me. I talk to him. I'm offering everything. He wants to see what the leaders will say. They don't want to surrender. They want to take that path that I left open out of Vinkovci. I didn't want to suffer any losses myself or inflict any losses on them at this point in time since Vukovar had already fallen. And then there was a lot of commotion. Why weren't the prisoners there? And then the telegram came, the one that was mentioned, and so on and so forth. And then the new assignments came up. Fill up, don't let them pull out. Where are they? Why are they there? And then all the other things that turned up. Whoever surrendered to us eventually surrendered. This was done in compliance with all regulations and the same would have been the case vice versa, and I was personally involved in this to make sure that the rules were complied with. After the conversation with Vesna Bosanac, there was this sudden change and indifferent delegations kept arriving. The security delegation from Sid, the delegation from the 1st Military District, the men from the cabinet, and what do I know? A whole lot of officers, anyway. Too many cooks spoil the broth. You know the old saying, and that's what happened in the end. My officers will hear me, I'm sure. I would like to take this opportunity to thank them for their -- for their courage, to thank them for the honourable way in which they fought. It was thanks to our excellent relationships that we were successful in carrying out our task and completing our mission. I also wish to recognise the effort made by the defenders of the time who had suffered a great many casualties. I don't know what they got from it in the end. So many lives were lost. I'm sure the problem could have been resolved in a different way. Finally, what I wish to say is this: I am sorry for my own officers, for my own COs, for my troops, all those who fought in the area. They were volunteers there and all sorts of other units as well. I am sorry for the common folks who lived in the area. I am sorry for the citizens of Vukovar, their defenders, their own citizens, people that I at one time lived with. I lived there for four years when I still went to school. I first fell in love there, of all places. My officers knew that. They respected the fact. It's a been a long time and now I realise that all of this was just a pure act of madness that should never have happened. The one essential issue that needs to be raised is this, and this is something that we've been discussing all along: Why did Ovcara occur? I'm asking the question now. I'll still be asking the question once this trial is over. Who stood to profit from this? Why did this have to happen, and so on and so forth. All I can say is, I am sorry it ever happened. If I'd known that it would happen, I would have prevented it. I wouldn't have left for Belgrade. I would have stuck around. I would have dealt with it. Nonetheless, this is just proof that there was no sort of joint criminal enterprise at all. It was never our intention for this to happen. When I say "we," I mean the three of us sitting here now as well as those back in Belgrade. Who is behind it is something that remains a mystery to me. Once again, I wish to thank the Honourable Chamber for lending me your ears. I think eventually the most important thing for a man is to be at peace with himself. One thing I do know is that I did not give that order. I didn't know that this would ever happen. It's not like I knew and did nothing to prevent it. Regardless of the eventual sentence, what I think is really important is this, that I can still live with myself in the knowledge that I knew nothing about this. Once again, thank you, Your Honours, for lending me your ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: And Mr. Radic also wants to say something. Mr. Radic. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a couple of words. It was through my Defence team that I expressed my regret for the victims. I denied my involvement in any of the crimes that occurred there. I wish to thank the Chamber once again for hearing me out when I took the stand myself. I can only again say that I was in no way involved or responsible for any of the crimes that occurred. Thank you for everything. This is all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Mr. Sljivacanin? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have much to say. My team has already put forward all of my own positions on my behalf. I told you about how I perceived the break-up of Yugoslavia, my country, the sufferings of people who were innocent, and the large-scale tragedy of young JNA soldiers. I took the stand. I told my story. I remained on that stand for eight days. I answered all of the questions that were asked. I invited honourable and responsible officers of the JNA and the Guards Brigade to testify here. They were eyewitnesses to everything that in those evil times I was compelled to do in Vukovar and what I eventually did. Unfortunately, on Wednesday we heard from Mr. Moore and on Thursday from Mr. Vasic, I'm not sure based on what, that all those men were liars, that they were trying to pin the blame on someone else. No, gentlemen. Those men were here for the truth, and they were not intimidated by the threats made by the Prosecution to include them in the joint criminal enterprise. Once again, I have to remind you of this: On the 21st of November, 1991, on the evening of the 21st, I parted ways with Mr. Borsinger as friends. I felt this way then, and I still feel that way. I wish you had called him, Mr. Moore, to check what I am saying. I believe that everyone in this courtroom and all honourable and sincere people just want to know the truth. All I have done has been for the truth to finally come out about the tragedy that occurred in 1991. There can be no greater punishment for me or to anyone than to lose my own country, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, than to witness the suffering of my own people, young soldiers and officers, to face enormous media pressure directed against my person. But believe me, what I have been hearing over the last two days spelt the end of me. Those were accusations and slander based on not a single fact. I am certain that I have fulfilled my promise from the opening statement, from the introduction, that my truth will be your truth at the end of this trial, Your Honours. I wasn't raised to discriminate along ethnic or racial lines. I was not raised to hate my own people. I was not raised to destroy my own country. Croats, too, were my people. Croatia, too, was my country at the time. It wasn't before I came here that I found out from the OTP that the distinction that had been drawn at the time was Serbs and non-Serbs. I don't understand where in this great scheme of things we have place for Montenegrins, like me, for example. Serbs, non-Serbs, Croats and everybody else who lived in Yugoslavia shared the same country, the same home, Yugoslavia. The world knew us. The world remembered us. However, history was not kind to them. A whirlwind came and blew them all away. Moves made by politicians that were impossible to explain brought these peoples to the brink of existence. This was their destiny. It was the destiny of their souls, but there was also a legal provision in the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, which I will now quote: "The armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia must protect the freedom, independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the country." Thank you. In this dark realm, in this tragical archetype, one thing that was demonstrated was this: If you comply with the constitution of the SFRY, you will be sorry; if you fail to comply, you will be sorry too. I fail to understand Mr. Moore or Mr. Vasic, what exactly they base their theories and what occurred in Vukovar on. I regret this. Gentleman, you can go on making things up any way you like, but you can never erase the truth about my humanitarian, about my readiness to sacrifice myself for the sake of the good, for the sake of the truth, nor can you do anything to sway my love for Yugoslavia and all of its peoples. I've done that in my introduction, but I have to do it again. I would like to express my deepest regret to all the victims of the Vukovar tragedy. I categorically condemn all those who occurred, such a heinous and atrocious crime thereby inflicting an intolerable wrong on their own people and inflicting grief on the families of those killed or maimed. Your Honours, I have every confidence that this Trial Chamber will rule in a just way. I expect a verdict from you that will be founded on facts and that will be founded on evidence, evidence of the sufferings at Ovcara. The truth is needed by all those who are not afraid of the truth. The truth is badly needed by the families of the victims, the families of the soldiers who were killed. It is also the Guards Brigade that needs the truth. All honourable, honest, and sincere people of Yugoslavia need to know the truth, especially the people of Serbia and the people of Croatia. I need the truth. My family needs the truth. And so do my friends. I expect a just verdict to clear my name and to clear the names of the honourable officers of the Guards Brigade. I served the Guards Brigade honourably. I acted in accordance with the laws and the oath which I have taken. Please don't hold it against me. I think it was by an act of omission that my lawyer forgot to say this: I would like to thank the staff at Bronovo hospital and the university clinic at Leiden who treated me and thereby enabled me to see this trial through to its conclusion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sljivacanin. This brings this trial to an end. The Trial Chamber also on behalf of Judge Parker wishes to thank counsel for the care with which they have prepared their cases, for the good spirit in which these proceedings have been conducted, which has also allowed us to proceed more speedily and more efficiently. So we are very grateful to everyone for that. I also want to express my appreciation to all those who have been working behind the scenes, the many people who have supported this trial. I think of the interpreters, I think of registry, I think of the translators, I think of the stenographists, and maybe I am still forgetting other persons. We will adjourn now and we will deliver our judgement in due course.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.35 p.m.
